title: Renewal Processes and Long-Run Reward
engineName: Track repeated renewals using inter-arrival times, renewal counts and long-run averages.
objectives: Define a renewal process from iid positive inter-renewal times.
Construct renewal epochs and the counting process N(t).
Distinguish inter-arrival time, renewal count and renewal function.
Use the renewal equation and elementary renewal theorem in elementary cases.

prereq.name: IID random variables
prereq.why: Successive gaps are iid in the ordinary renewal model.

prereq.name: Expectation and distribution functions
prereq.why: Renewal counts and long-run rates use expectations and distribution functions.

prereq.name: Poisson process
prereq.why: A Poisson process is a special renewal process with exponential gaps.

traps: Renewal epochs are cumulative sums, not individual gaps.
N(t) counts renewals by t; m(t)=E[N(t)] is the renewal function.
The long-run renewal rate is 1/μ, not μ.
The elementary renewal theorem is asymptotic, not an exact finite-time formula.
howto: Define iid positive gaps Xᵢ; form Sₙ=ΣXᵢ; count N(t)=max{n:Sₙ≤t}; calculate μ=E[X]; use 1/μ for long-run renewal rate and E[R]/μ for long-run reward.

sheet: X₁,X₂,… are iid positive inter-renewal times with mean μ=E[X₁].
Exponential iid gaps give a Poisson process.
tricks: Draw the timeline before counting N(t).
Include an event exactly at t because Sₙ≤t.
Invert the mean gap for the long-run rate.
Do not use the Poisson count formula for a general renewal process.
shortcuts: Exponential gaps of rate λ: E[N(t)]=λt.
remember: IID gaps are central to the ordinary renewal model.
Long-run results do not determine all finite-time probabilities.

scenes.title: Refresh cumulative waiting times
body: Successive cycle lengths are X₁,X₂,… . The time of the second event is S₂=X₁+X₂; the time of the nth event is Sₙ=X₁+⋯+Xₙ.
A gap is a duration. An epoch is the cumulative time at which an event occurs.

items.ask: If gaps are 3 and 5 hours, when does renewal 2 occur?
refresh: Add the first two cycle lengths.
An epoch is cumulative time, not a gap.

items.ask: If X₁=2, X₂=4 and X₃=1, find S₃.
refresh: S₃ is the third cumulative epoch.

items.ask: If X is 1 or 3 with equal probability, find E[X].
refresh: Weight each value by its probability.

scenes.title: A system that renews repeatedly
body: A renewal may represent replacing a failed component, completing a repair or replenishing stock. Each renewal begins a fresh cycle.
The ordinary model assumes cycle lengths are iid positive random variables. If the distribution changes from cycle to cycle, the ordinary model may not apply.

scenario.title: Count completed service cycles
body: The times between component replacements are X₁,X₂,… . The third replacement occurs at S₃=X₁+X₂+X₃.
The ordinary model assumes iid positive cycle lengths. If ageing changes the distribution from cycle to cycle, this model may not apply.
scenario.q: What does one renewal cycle measure?
scenario.answer: The time from one renewal to the next.

scenes.title: Formal definition of a renewal process
body: Let X₁,X₂,… be iid positive inter-renewal times with distribution F and finite mean μ=E[X₁] when finite-mean results are used.
Renewal epochs: S₀=0 and Sₙ=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ. Counting process: N(t)=max{n:Sₙ≤t}. Renewal function: m(t)=E[N(t)].

scenes.title: Worked example: deterministic gaps
body: If every inter-renewal time is c=4 hours, then S₁=4, S₂=8 and S₃=12.
At t=11, exactly two epochs have occurred, so N(11)=2. The definition includes events exactly at t.
scenes.problem: A component is replaced exactly every 4 hours. Find S₁,S₂,S₃ and N(11).

scenes.title: Renewal counts and their distribution
body: N(t)≥n if and only if Sₙ≤t. Exactly n renewals means Sₙ≤t<Sₙ₊₁.
For random gaps, the cumulative epochs and therefore the number of renewals by a fixed t are random.

scenes.title: Worked example: exponential gaps
body: If iid gaps are exponential with rate λ, the renewal counting process is a homogeneous Poisson process.
For λ=3 per hour and t=2 hours, E[N(2)]=λt=6. This formula is specific to exponential gaps.
scenes.problem: Inter-renewal times are iid exponential with rate 3 per hour. Find E[N(2)].

steps.say: Exponential iid gaps define a Poisson process.
steps.why: This is the special renewal model.
The expected count equals rate times duration.

scenes.title: The renewal equation
body: Let F(t)=P(X₁≤t). The renewal function satisfies m(t)=F(t)+∫₀ᵗm(t−x)dF(x).
Condition on the first gap x: if the first renewal occurs at x, the remaining time is t−x and the expected subsequent count is m(t−x).

scenes.title: Fixed gaps versus random gaps
body: A deterministic gap gives regular epochs and N(t)=⌊t/c⌋. Random gaps create variable spacing.
Two models can have the same mean gap but different finite-time count distributions. The mean alone does not determine every finite-time probability.

scenes.title: Elementary renewal theorem
body: Under standard conditions for iid positive gaps with finite mean μ, the elementary renewal theorem states m(t)/t→1/μ as t→∞.
The long-run renewal rate is the reciprocal of the mean cycle length. This is an asymptotic result, not an exact finite-time formula.

scenes.title: Guided problem: long-run rate
body: Let X be 1 hour with probability 1/4 and 3 hours with probability 3/4. Then μ=1/4+9/4=5/2 hours.
The long-run rate is 1/μ=2/5 renewals per hour. The mean gap is a time; its reciprocal is a rate.
scenes.problem: X is 1 hour with probability 1/4 and 3 hours with probability 3/4. Find the long-run renewal rate.
solution: The elementary renewal theorem gives rate 1/μ.
The rate is 2/5 renewals per hour.

scenes.title: Renewal-reward theorem
body: If R is the reward earned in one cycle and X is its length, the renewal-reward theorem gives long-run reward per unit time E[R]/E[X], under standard iid-cycle and integrability conditions.
Use expected reward per cycle divided by expected cycle duration.

scenes.title: Guided problem: reward rate
body: A system earns expected reward 100 units per cycle and has expected cycle duration 5 hours.
The long-run reward rate is 100/5=20 units per hour.
scenes.problem: Expected reward per cycle is 100 units and expected cycle duration is 5 hours. Find the long-run reward rate.
solution: Divide expected reward per cycle by expected cycle duration.

scenes.title: Exam traps and interpretation checks
body: Renewal epochs are cumulative sums, N(t) is a count, and m(t)=E[N(t)] is an expected count.
The long-run rate is 1/μ, not μ. A Poisson process is a special renewal process, not the only renewal process.
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false.

items.why: Sₙ is the sum of the first n gaps.

items.claim: N(t) counts renewals completed by t.
items.why: It counts epochs not exceeding t.
Only exponential iid gaps give the Poisson process.

scenes.title: Summary and supplementary status
scenes.objective: Recall the key results and scope.
body: Start with iid positive gaps; form Sₙ; count N(t); and distinguish the random count from m(t)=E[N(t)].

The elementary renewal theorem gives rate 1/E[X]. The renewal-reward theorem gives E[R]/E[X]. This lesson is supplementary: renewal processes are not explicitly named in the official Unit IX syllabus shared for this project.
